passages.title: Cooling the city, one street at a time

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Urban heat is often discussed as if it were a single temperature covering an entire city. Yet a person waiting beside a broad road may experience very different conditions from someone sitting in a nearby shaded courtyard. Sunlight warms roofs and paving; these surfaces then release stored energy after sunset. The term urban heat island describes the contrast between built areas and their rural surroundings, but that average can conceal important differences within the city. For people planning short walking routes, street-level conditions may matter more than the city-wide figure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In a small, fictional pilot in the city of Merrow, planners compared twelve streets rather than choosing one showcase neighbourhood. Sensors were mounted at pedestrian height, and a mobile team repeated measurements at the same time on comparable summer days. The investigators recorded air temperature as well as the temperature of nearby surfaces. They also asked walkers where they felt comfortable. These measures did not always agree: an exposed pavement could feel unpleasant even when a nearby air sensor registered only a modest change. The pilot was designed to guide local decisions, not establish a universal cooling figure.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Trees were useful, but counting them was a poor substitute for mapping their shade. A young tree and a mature tree each counted as one item in the inventory, despite offering very different protection. The time of day mattered too. A canopy that sheltered a morning queue might leave an afternoon bus stop exposed. Merrow therefore mapped shade at hourly intervals. The resulting maps helped planners identify gaps along routes to schools and clinics, where even a short stretch without shelter could discourage walking.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another proposal involved reflective paving, which sends a greater proportion of incoming sunlight away from the ground. This can reduce surface temperature. However, a cooler surface does not necessarily mean a more comfortable pedestrian: reflected radiation can reach the body or nearby windows. The team recommended testing a small area and gathering feedback before committing an entire street to the material. They rejected the idea of ranking every cooling measure by a single number, because its effects depended on where it was installed and who used the space.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Maintenance placed limits on the planting scheme. Some locations lacked enough soil for roots, and new trees needed watering during establishment. A grant could pay for planting while leaving no dependable budget for later care. The council therefore required a five-year maintenance plan before approving each group of trees. In the pilot, residents reported comfort and access problems, but they were not responsible for technical inspections. Their observations complemented professional checks rather than replacing them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The final proposal combined shaded routes, selective planting and modest trials of new paving. It prioritised access to essential services over producing an impressive total number of trees. A public dashboard displayed observations and the uncertainty around them. The authors argued that a useful heat strategy should be assessed by the journeys it makes possible, as well as by environmental measurements. They did not claim that the pilot would remove the need for wider efforts to reduce emissions.

passages.title: What a seed bank can and cannot save

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A seed bank is often described as a library for future agriculture. The comparison is helpful because both depend on careful cataloguing and continued access, but seeds are living material rather than stable pages. Collections must be checked and, when necessary, regenerated by growing plants and harvesting a fresh generation. Keeping seeds cold and dry can slow deterioration; it cannot make every sample immortal. A package in a freezer is therefore the beginning of a conservation process, not its completion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many crop species produce orthodox seeds, which tolerate drying and low temperatures. Other species produce seeds that are damaged by those conditions. Such collections may require living plants or techniques that preserve small pieces of plant tissue. The choice is biological rather than merely financial: buying a larger freezer will not make unsuitable seeds tolerate conventional storage. A conservation programme may consequently use several methods for different species, rather than selecting one technology for everything.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Documentation is another essential resource. If a sample lacks reliable information about where it was collected, researchers may struggle to decide how to use it. A hillside population and a lowland population of the same species can carry different traits. Labels also need to survive staff changes and software replacement. In a fictional regional collection at Alder Farm, curators kept both digital records and printed summaries. The printed copies were a precaution against temporary access problems, not a claim that paper records could replace the full database.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Access involves people as well as storage. Farmers who maintain diverse crops in their fields continually select plants for local conditions and preferences. Their knowledge can help curators interpret a collection, while the bank may supply material after a local loss. However, the two approaches are not interchangeable. A stored collection captures particular samples; a farming population continues to change. Agreements about sharing material and recognising contributors are therefore part of conservation, rather than administrative details to be considered only at the end.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Before releasing a small sample to a researcher, a bank may check whether enough viable seeds remain. Germination tests use a portion of the collection, so staff must balance information gained against material consumed. If viability falls, regeneration may be necessary. But growing a new generation carelessly can itself change the collection: only plants that flower under the chosen conditions will contribute seeds. Curators therefore document the conditions and try to preserve the range represented by the original sample.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Seed banks offer valuable insurance against loss, but insurance is not a substitute for maintaining habitats and farming knowledge. A diverse collection can expand future options without predicting exactly which trait a future crop will need. The strongest argument for this work is not that every stored sample will be used. It is that a range of possibilities should remain available. Assessing success solely by the number of packets stored risks rewarding accumulation while neglecting viability, documentation and fair access.

passages.title: The hidden work of making research repeatable

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A surprising result attracts attention, but the work needed to check it is often less visible. Repeating a study can reveal whether a finding depends on a particular sample, an analytical decision or an unnoticed feature of the original setting. It does not follow that a result which fails to repeat was fraudulent. Small samples, random variation and differences in measurement can all matter. Treating every unsuccessful repetition as proof of dishonesty discourages the careful comparisons that research needs.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For clarity, some researchers distinguish reproducing an analysis from replicating a study. Reproduction in this sense means using the same data and code to see whether the published result can be obtained. Replication collects new data to test a related question. Terminology varies across disciplines, so a report should state what was actually done instead of relying only on a label. A reader needs to know whether new participants were recruited, whether the original materials were used and which choices were changed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sharing a spreadsheet is not always sufficient. Variables may have unclear names, missing values may be coded in unusual ways, or a processing step may exist only in a former researcher’s memory. A data dictionary explains what each variable represents and how it was measured. Versioned code records changes to analysis, while a record of software dependencies helps another team reconstruct the environment. These practices require time, especially when a project was not organised for sharing from the beginning.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In a fictional study of library reminders, two teams tested whether a message increased the return of overdue books. Team North sent messages in the morning; Team South sent them in the evening. Their results differed. Rather than immediately attributing the gap to time of day, the teams compared who received the messages, how overdue was defined and whether the notices were successfully delivered. Only a controlled comparison could separate these possible explanations. A plausible story about a difference was not itself a test of that story.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Preregistration can help by recording a question and an analysis plan before the results are examined. It makes it easier to distinguish planned tests from exploratory ones. Exploration remains valuable: an unexpected pattern may suggest a better question. The problem arises when an exploratory finding is presented as though it had been predicted all along. Preregistration also cannot guarantee that a measurement is meaningful or that a sample represents the population. Transparency is useful without being a complete quality certificate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Incentives shape whether these practices become routine. If institutions reward only novel positive findings, researchers have little time for careful verification. Journals, funders and employers can recognise well-designed replications, shared methods and the maintenance of reusable datasets. The author’s proposal is not to replace discovery with checking, but to treat both as necessary parts of cumulative knowledge. A field becomes more trustworthy when uncertainty can be examined openly rather than hidden behind a tidy final narrative.

passages.title: Libraries beyond the book count

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A public library can lend fewer printed books while becoming more useful to its community. This possibility complicates the familiar practice of measuring performance mainly through circulation figures. Some visitors come for quiet study, others for internet access, language groups or help with unfamiliar forms. These activities do not make books irrelevant. They show that one transaction count cannot represent the full range of services that a shared public space provides.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the fictional town of Westhaven, librarians began their review by observing how different rooms were used. They recorded occupancy at several points during the day rather than only at closing time. The large reading room was busiest after school, while small meeting rooms were more popular in the mornings. A survey then asked visitors what had brought them in. Staff avoided collecting names because the purpose was service planning, not tracking individual readers. Even so, they recognised that the survey would miss people who never entered the building.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Non-users offered a different perspective. Some could not visit during opening hours; others found the entrance difficult to navigate or assumed that all services required a paid membership. The library tested a later opening on one evening each week and improved signs near the entrance. It also explained which services were free. These changes addressed identified barriers, but staff did not assume that a single trial would resolve every reason for staying away. They planned to review participation before making the extended hours permanent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Digital services introduced a further complication. An online renewal saved a trip, but the number of renewals said little about whether a reader could find useful information. Meanwhile, staff spent time helping visitors judge the reliability of websites. This work was hard to reduce to a simple count. The review combined short visitor accounts with service statistics, while removing details that could identify individuals. A personal story could illustrate an issue without being treated as proof that every visitor had the same experience.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Changes to space required negotiation. Quiet study and lively group activities could conflict when placed too close together. Instead of declaring one type of use more valuable, staff created quieter zones and scheduled some group sessions outside peak study hours. Flexible furniture helped, but moving tables alone could not solve poor sound separation. The building’s physical limits meant that not every activity could be accommodated at the same time. Clear information about where and when to find each service became part of the solution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Westhaven’s report retained book loans as one indicator while adding measures of access, participation and user experience. It warned against equating a busy room with a successful service: overcrowding may signal inadequate provision. Equally, a small specialist session may offer substantial value to a few people. The report argued for interpreting numbers in context and revisiting them as needs changed. Its goal was a library that could explain why its choices helped the public, rather than simply report the largest possible totals.

passages.title: Repairing a product, preserving a choice

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Repair is sometimes presented as a simple matter of persuading owners to keep products longer. Motivation matters, but a willing owner may still face practical barriers. A replacement part might be unavailable, a case difficult to open, or instructions limited to authorised workshops. Whether a product remains in use therefore depends on a system of design, information, skills and incentives. Asking only whether consumers care about waste overlooks many of the choices made before a device reaches them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A repairability score tries to make some of these barriers visible before purchase. Depending on its design, it might consider access to parts, the tools needed for disassembly and the availability of instructions. Yet a single score compresses several different issues. One buyer may need a battery replacement, while another is concerned about a broken screen. A transparent scoring system should therefore show its components rather than hide them behind a large number on a label. Consumers can then judge which features matter for the way they use the product.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Independent workshops provide expertise that many owners lack. In the fictional district of Elmbrook, a community repair event paired volunteers with residents, but it excluded work on mains electrical components. Organisers described the event as a place to learn basic diagnosis and safe maintenance, not a replacement for qualified specialists. Participants were encouraged to explain the fault before anyone opened a case. Sometimes the apparent failure was a setting or a damaged cable rather than the main device, so careful diagnosis could avoid unnecessary intervention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Parts supply remained a difficulty even for skilled repairers. A cheap component might be sold only as part of a much larger assembly. This could make replacement expensive and waste functioning material. Standard fasteners and modular parts could reduce such problems, although modular design also involves trade-offs in size, weight and manufacturing. The passage does not assume that every modular product will last longer; durable construction and continuing support still matter. Design choices should be assessed against actual repair needs rather than promoted as universal solutions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Software can determine a product’s useful life as strongly as hardware. A device that still works physically may lose important functions when updates or associated services stop. Clear information about the support period helps buyers make a decision before purchase. It does not guarantee that every future threat can be solved, but it makes an important dependency visible. A repair policy that considers only screws and spare parts may therefore overlook a major cause of premature replacement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Repair is not automatically the best environmental option in every case. An old appliance may use much more energy than a suitable replacement, and the balance depends on how often it is used, how it is powered and what producing a new model requires. Claims should compare the whole situation rather than assume that either repair or replacement always wins. For many everyday products, however, removing unnecessary barriers gives owners a choice they currently lack. The aim is to enable an informed decision, not impose a single answer on every household.

passages.title: Why a forecast needs more than a number

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A forecast can be useful without being certain. Weather services, transport planners and public-health teams all make decisions before the future is known. A single predicted value is easy to communicate, but it can conceal the range of outcomes that remain plausible. For someone deciding whether to protect equipment from rain, the chance of a severe event may matter more than the most likely rainfall total. Good forecasting is therefore connected to the decision being made, not simply to the appeal of a precise-looking number.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One method uses an ensemble: a collection of model runs with varied starting conditions or assumptions. If these runs produce different outcomes, their spread can reveal sensitivity to uncertainty. However, agreement does not prove accuracy. All members may share a missing process or a biased input. A narrow range can then create confidence without justification. Forecast designers need to compare predictions with later observations, not merely admire agreement among models. Variety has value when it captures meaningful differences, rather than cosmetic changes to the same assumptions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Calibration asks whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies over many comparable cases. If events assigned a probability of seventy per cent occur roughly seventy per cent of the time, that set of forecasts is well calibrated in this respect. It does not mean that any individual event was guaranteed. Nor is calibration the only useful property: a forecast that always gives a broad average may fail to distinguish high-risk situations from ordinary ones. Users also need information that changes appropriately when conditions change.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In a fictional coastal authority, two teams considered closing a waterfront path. The maintenance team cared about damage to temporary barriers, while the visitor team cared about safe access. They agreed to discuss consequences and available actions before selecting a warning threshold. Closing too often had costs, but failing to close during a dangerous event had different and potentially larger consequences. A decision threshold was therefore not simply a scientific constant; it reflected responsibilities, resources and the severity of possible harm.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Communication shaped the response. A coloured map attracted attention, but some residents interpreted the boundary of a warning area as an exact physical border. The authority added a short explanation that conditions changed gradually and local exposure varied. It also stated when the forecast would be updated. Providing uncertainty did not require listing every possible outcome. It required explaining which differences mattered and what people could reasonably do next, while making clear that new observations could alter the advice.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: After each event, staff reviewed both the forecast and the decision. A sensible precaution could be followed by harmless weather; that alone did not prove the precaution unreasonable. Equally, a lucky outcome could conceal poor reasoning. The review used information available at the time, along with later observations, to improve future practice. The broader lesson is that judging a forecast solely by whether one dramatic event happened confuses the quality of a process with the result of a single uncertain case.

passages.title: Part 1 · Joining a community workshop

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part one. A visitor is asking about a community workshop. Read questions one to ten before listening.

Receptionist: Hello, welcome to the Riverside workshop centre. How can I help?
Visitor: I would like to join the practical course. I saw an advertisement for painting, but it is actually the pottery course that interests me.
Receptionist: Certainly. May I take your surname?
Visitor: It is Bennett. That is B, E, N, N, E, T, T. The final letter is T.
Receptionist: Thank you. The next course starts on the fourteenth of May. The old leaflet says the seventh, but that session has been moved.
Visitor: The fourteenth is fine. Is it held every Monday?
Receptionist: No, that is the advanced group. Your group meets on Thursday. Classes begin at six thirty in the evening. We suggest arriving a little earlier the first time, so you can find the room.
Visitor: And how much does the course cost? Someone mentioned sixty pounds.
Receptionist: Sixty is the reduced student price. The standard fee for the whole course is seventy-five pounds. That includes the tools and clay. You do not need to purchase those separately.
Visitor: I am not a student, so I will pay the standard fee. Should I bring anything with me?
Receptionist: Please bring an apron. We provide tools, but your clothes may get dirty. Some visitors bring gloves, though those are not required.
Visitor: Where exactly is the classroom?
Receptionist: It is in the garden studio. Go past the main office and follow the path. The upstairs studio is used for drawing, so do not go there.
Visitor: Can I come by bus?
Receptionist: Yes, take the number twenty-four. It stops outside the centre. The number forty-two goes to a different part of town.
Visitor: Wonderful. I have never done this before. Is that a problem?
Receptionist: Not at all. This group is for beginners. You can move to the intermediate class later if you wish. I will reserve your place and send the payment instructions today.
Visitor: Thank you very much.
This is the end of part one. Check your answers.

passages.title: Part 2 · A visitor centre tour

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part two. A guide introduces a visitor centre. Read the questions before listening.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Meadow visitor centre. Before you explore, I will explain how the site works. The building opens at nine, but our first guided walk starts at ten. Please do not confuse the opening time with the walk time. If you want to join, register here at reception rather than waiting outside.
The walk takes ninety minutes. Some older notices describe a two-hour route, but that path is closed for maintenance. Our current route is shorter and avoids the steep steps. It is suitable for people who prefer a gentle walk, although everyone should wear suitable shoes.
Now, imagine a simple plan of the centre. You are standing in the entrance at the southern end. Immediately to your left is the cafe. On your right is the shop, where local artists sell postcards and small prints. If you walk straight ahead from the entrance, the exhibition room is at the north end of the corridor. Do visit it before you leave; it explains how the nearby river has changed.
You can borrow binoculars from the desk beside the exhibition room. We do not charge for borrowing them, but you need to leave a deposit of ten pounds. It is returned when you bring the equipment back. Please return everything before four thirty, when the equipment desk closes.
If you have brought children, there is a special activity this afternoon. They will make paper birds, not wooden boats as announced last month. The session starts after lunch and is supervised by two members of staff. Each child should still be accompanied by an adult.
There is also a short talk for adults about river restoration. It will be given by a local ecologist. She will discuss recent changes to the riverbank and explain which observations visitors can contribute. You do not need any scientific training to attend.
One final request: the outdoor path can be muddy after rain. Please wear boots if you have them. There is no need to bring a helmet because we are walking, not cycling. Maps are available on this desk, and I am happy to answer questions. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.
This is the end of part two.

passages.title: Part 3 · Planning a student investigation

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part three. Two students discuss a research assignment with their tutor.

Tutor: You have chosen a topic for the assignment. Tell me how it has developed.
Maya: We first considered food waste in student kitchens. But we could not get reliable access to the kitchens, so we changed the topic to bicycle parking on campus.
Leo: We want to know why people leave bicycles outside the marked spaces. There may not be enough spaces, or the existing ones may be inconvenient.
Tutor: Good. How will you collect evidence?
Maya: We will begin with observations at different times, rather than sending out a questionnaire immediately. That should show us where the problem actually occurs.
Tutor: Which locations will you use?
Leo: Three sites: the library, the sports centre and the science building. We considered the main gate, but the construction work there would distort the results.
Maya: At each site we will observe for thirty minutes in the morning and again in the afternoon. A full hour at each visit would be difficult with our class schedule.
Tutor: How long will the study run?
Leo: Two weeks. A single day would be too dependent on the weather. We will record weather conditions as part of the observation sheet.
Tutor: You should test that sheet first.
Maya: Yes, we plan a pilot on Friday. It should reveal whether our categories are clear enough. We may need to distinguish bicycles attached to railings from bicycles blocking a path.
Tutor: What about asking users why they parked there?
Leo: We could conduct short interviews after the pilot, if the ethics process allows it. We will not collect names. The information sheet explains that participation is voluntary.
Tutor: Remember that people may give answers they think you want. Compare interviews with observations instead of treating either as the whole picture.
Maya: For the presentation, we thought of using a table for every measurement.
Tutor: A table is useful in the appendix, but a map will make the location differences clearer in the main presentation.
Leo: That makes sense. When is the final report due?
Tutor: The draft is due on the twelfth of June, and the final version on the nineteenth. Do not confuse the two dates. Please send the observation sheet before your pilot, so I can comment on it.
This is the end of part three.

paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part four. A lecturer discusses rain gardens. The lecture is a simplified teaching example, not a report of a real study.

Today I will discuss small urban landscapes designed to manage rainwater. A rain garden is a shallow planted depression that temporarily holds runoff. Unlike a decorative pond, it is not intended to remain filled with water permanently. The water gradually soaks into the soil, and the plants tolerate alternating wet and dry conditions.
The primary aim is to reduce runoff entering drains during rainfall. That can help a drainage system cope with short periods of heavy flow. A rain garden should not, however, be described as a solution to every kind of flooding. Its performance depends on the site, the soil and the volume of water reaching it.
Site selection begins with understanding the soil. A simple infiltration test measures how readily water enters the ground. Where infiltration is poor, the design may need an underdrain or a different location. Positioning a garden close to a building without checking local guidance could create problems, so technical advice remains important.
The surface is planted, but much of the work happens below it. A layer of gravel may provide space for temporary water storage and support drainage. Designers must consider where excess water will go during a very large storm. An overflow route sends that water to a planned destination rather than allowing it to find an accidental path.
Plant choice also matters. Native plants can be suitable when their needs match the conditions, but the label native alone is not enough. The design must consider tolerance of both short wet periods and longer dry periods. In our fictional demonstration garden, the team chose a mixture of grasses and flowering plants rather than a single species.
Maintenance is often underestimated. Litter can block the inlet, which is the point where runoff enters. Removing that litter and checking the inlet after storms helps keep the system working. Staff also inspect for erosion and replace failed plants when necessary. These tasks need a named person or team, not just a note in the original design.
Finally, evaluation should look at several outcomes. Measuring water levels can show how quickly the garden drains. Recording maintenance hours reveals the work required. Observing insects may provide information about habitat value, although one visit cannot describe an entire season. A useful report should combine these observations and state the limits of its evidence. The garden is part of a wider drainage strategy, not a substitute for every other measure.
This is the end of part four.

passages.title: Part 1 · Reserving a study room

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part one. A student calls a university building to reserve a room.

Assistant: Good afternoon, learning centre reception.
Student: Hello. I need a room for a small project meeting. My surname is Patel, P, A, T, E, L. I have used the centre before, but not the meeting rooms.
Assistant: When would you like to come?
Student: On the twenty-second of October. We originally planned the twenty-first, but one member has a laboratory class that day.
Assistant: There is a room available at two fifteen in the afternoon. The two o'clock slot is already booked.
Student: Two fifteen will work. There will be six of us. We might invite another student next week, but only six will attend this meeting.
Assistant: Then the Cedar room should be suitable. It has eight chairs, so you will have enough space. The smaller Birch room only has four.
Student: Is a projector available?
Assistant: Yes. I will reserve one for you. The screen is fixed in the room. Please bring your own laptop, because we do not lend those for meetings.
Student: Fine. Where do I collect the key?
Assistant: From the security desk, not this reception. The security desk is beside the east entrance. You will need to show your student card when you collect it.
Student: How long can we stay?
Assistant: The maximum booking is two hours. You can book a shorter session, but you cannot go beyond two hours because another group may need the room.
Student: Is there any fee?
Assistant: Not for registered students. If you no longer need the booking, please give us at least twenty-four hours' notice. We can then offer it to somebody else.
Student: I will let you know. Could you send the details in writing?
Assistant: Of course. The confirmation will be sent by email, usually within an hour. Check your spam folder if it does not arrive. Please reply if the date or time is wrong, and we will correct it.
Student: Thank you for your help.
This is the end of part one.

passages.title: Part 2 · Helping at the local museum

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part two. A museum coordinator welcomes new volunteers.

Welcome to the local history museum. I am glad you can help us this season. Your first training session will be on Saturday. We considered Sunday, but the trainer is unavailable then. Please come to the education room, which is upstairs beside the small library.
The entrance for volunteers is on the west side of the building. Visitors use the main entrance at the front, but it may still be locked when you arrive. The west door opens earlier. Ring the bell if no member of staff is there to welcome you.
During training, you will receive a blue badge. Please wear it whenever you are volunteering, so visitors know whom to approach. Green badges are for our permanent staff. If you lose your badge, tell the coordinator rather than borrowing somebody else's.
Your initial shift will last three hours. We ask new volunteers not to sign up for a full day until they know the role. There will be time for a break, and you can use the staff kitchen for drinks. The cafe is for visitors and can get busy at lunchtime.
Photography is allowed in most rooms, but flash is not permitted because some objects are sensitive to light. If visitors ask you about photographs, please explain that distinction. Do not tell them that all photography is banned.
For questions about access or facilities, use the radio. A member of staff can give current information. Please do not leave a busy room unattended to search for someone. If a visitor has lost something, send them to reception, where staff keep the lost property record.
We encourage you to ask questions yourself. On your first visit, you will work with a mentor. This person can show you how to describe objects without touching them and how to respond when you do not know an answer. It is better to check than invent a fact about an object.
Finally, if you cannot attend your shift, contact us by telephone. Email is useful for routine questions, but we may not read it quickly enough on a busy morning. Please call as early as possible. Thank you for giving your time; your help makes the museum more welcoming.
This is the end of part two.

passages.title: Part 3 · Improving a survey

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part three. Two students review a survey with their supervisor.

Supervisor: Let us review the survey before you send it out. What question are you investigating?
Nora: How students use the campus cafe as a study space. At first we called the project student diet, but that was much broader than our actual questions.
Sam: Our respondents will be first-year students. We cannot claim that they represent every student, but this is the group our assignment focuses on.
Supervisor: How many responses do you hope to receive?
Nora: Eighty. We originally wrote one hundred and fifty in the plan, but that would be unrealistic in the time available. Eighty is our revised target, not a result we have already achieved.
Supervisor: Good distinction. Now, your second question asks whether the cafe is cheap and convenient. That combines two different judgments.
Sam: So we should separate them into two questions. A student might find it convenient but expensive.
Supervisor: Exactly. And avoid suggesting the answer. Ask neutrally rather than saying that the cafe is obviously too noisy.
Nora: We will include an option for people who never use it. Otherwise the survey might force them to express an opinion they do not have.
Supervisor: Test the revised form with a small group.
Sam: We can run the pilot with five students tomorrow. We will ask them to describe any question they find confusing.
Nora: For recruitment, we planned to approach people outside the cafe, but that could miss students who avoid it. We will use the course mailing list instead.
Supervisor: Remember to ask permission to use that list. Your introduction should explain the purpose, the time required and how responses will be used.
Sam: We estimate that completion will take four minutes. The pilot will help us check that estimate.
Nora: We will report results as percentages as well as actual counts, so readers can see the size of the sample. For the main figure, would a pie chart work?
Supervisor: A bar chart would make comparison between response categories easier. Explain how many people answered each question because some may leave items blank.
Sam: When do you need the revised survey?
Supervisor: By Wednesday, please. Then there will be time to comment before distribution. Do not start collecting full responses until the form has been approved.
This is the end of part three.

passages.title: Part 4 · Light and daily rhythms

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original listening exercise. Part four. A lecturer explains daily rhythms in a simplified teaching talk. This is not medical advice.

Today we are considering how light helps coordinate daily biological rhythms. A circadian rhythm is an approximately daily pattern. The word approximately is important: without environmental signals, an individual's internal cycle may not match exactly the twenty-four hours of the day. Light is one of the signals that helps the internal system stay aligned with the environment.
Information about light enters through the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. This does not mean that every response to light is the same as forming a visual image. Biological timing involves specialised pathways as well as ordinary sight. For our purposes, remember that timing depends on signals, not simply on deciding to feel awake.
The effect of light depends partly on its timing. Morning light and late-evening light can influence the daily cycle differently. Brightness and duration also matter, so it is misleading to discuss a device only by the colour of its screen. A short, dim exposure and a long, bright exposure are not equivalent situations.
In a fictional classroom demonstration, students kept a sleep diary for a week. The aim was to notice patterns, not diagnose a disorder. Each diary recorded bedtime, waking time and the student's sense of alertness. The group also noted caffeine use, because that could influence how awake people felt independently of the light conditions.
Wearable devices were discussed as another source of information. They can estimate activity and rest over time, but their measurements are not identical to a clinical sleep assessment. Students were asked to compare their diary with the device's output rather than assume the device was always correct. An apparent disagreement could reflect the limits of either source.
Consistency was another theme. A very different weekend schedule can complicate the relationship between social commitments and biological timing. Yet simply telling everyone to follow one schedule ignores shift work, caring responsibilities and individual variation. Public advice needs to recognise those constraints instead of blaming people for every difficulty.
Finally, the lecturer stressed uncertainty. The class demonstration was observational. It could identify associations, but it could not prove that one factor caused a change in sleep. A controlled experiment would require a more careful design. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep problems should seek appropriate professional advice rather than treat this teaching exercise as a diagnosis. The useful lesson is to record context, question simple explanations and distinguish a pattern from a causal conclusion.
This is the end of part four.

passages.title: The unexpected value of an imperfect translation

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A translated text can look so smooth that readers forget it has passed through another language. Fluency is often desirable, but it can conceal decisions. A word describing a family relationship may have no exact equivalent, and a polite request may sound unusually direct when moved into a different social setting. Translation therefore involves more than replacing vocabulary. Translators decide which information needs explaining, which ambiguity should remain, and how much unfamiliarity a reader can reasonably encounter without losing the thread.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In a fictional workshop, translator Mira Hale asked students to translate a short account of a neighbourhood meeting. One group replaced an unfamiliar local institution with a familiar organisation from their own country. Another retained the original term and added a brief explanation. Both versions were readable, but the first implied that the two institutions had identical responsibilities. Hale did not argue that unfamiliar terms should always remain. Her concern was that an apparently helpful substitution could introduce a factual claim the original text had never made.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Linguist Daniel Cho focused on a different difficulty: uncertainty. A witness in the workshop text described a vehicle using a word that could refer to several sizes of van. Some students chose a precise vehicle category, assuming that specificity made the writing more professional. Cho pointed out that this removed the witness's uncertainty. In a literary work such a change might alter the atmosphere; in an administrative record it might change how the evidence was interpreted. The problem was not poor grammar but an unsupported increase in precision.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Editor Salma Reed examined the purpose of the translated text. Visitors reading a safety notice needed to understand what action to take quickly, whereas researchers studying an old notice might need to know exactly how it was worded. A translation appropriate for one audience could be unsuitable for the other. Reed recommended writing a short brief before beginning: who would use the text, what they needed from it, and which features must be preserved. This brief could guide decisions without pretending to settle every difficult case in advance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Machine translation added another layer to the exercise. Students were given a fluent automated draft containing a mistaken relationship between two people. Several corrected minor stylistic details while leaving the relationship untouched. The workshop team argued that fluency can direct attention towards the surface and away from meaning. They recommended checking names, relationships, quantities and logical connections against the source before polishing the style. This checking process required knowledge of both languages, rather than confidence in how convincing the draft sounded.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The final discussion did not produce a single rule for every translation. Instead, participants documented choices that materially affected meaning and explained them to a reviewer. Some decisions could remain invisible in the final text, but they should not be invisible in the working process. The workshop's broader lesson was that a good translation earns trust by serving a clear purpose and preserving relevant distinctions. Smooth reading is valuable; it becomes misleading when it persuades readers that no interpretation has taken place.

passages.title: How a coastline becomes an archive

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A coastline records change, but it does not do so like a book with numbered pages. Waves can remove sediment, storms can rearrange it, and people can move objects long after they were first deposited. An archaeological object found beside the sea therefore raises two questions: what it is and how it arrived at its present position. The second question can be harder. Without an account of the surrounding material, a striking object may tell researchers surprisingly little about the activity that once took place there.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At the fictional inlet of Greyhaven, an archaeological team surveyed an exposed wooden structure. Local residents had noticed it after a storm removed sand from the beach. The team first recorded its position and the layers around it rather than immediately lifting the wood. Their photographs included a scale, and their notes distinguished direct observations from interpretations. They could observe the arrangement of posts, for example, while the suggestion that the structure had supported a landing platform remained a hypothesis to be tested.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dating required several kinds of evidence. Tree rings could reveal when the wood grew, but growth date and construction date were not necessarily identical. Timber might have been stored, reused or taken from an older building. Objects in nearby sediment could also have moved from elsewhere. The researchers therefore compared evidence rather than selecting whichever date looked most precise. A narrow numerical estimate could still answer the wrong question if the relationship between the sample and the structure had been misunderstood.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Conservation presented a separate challenge. Wood that had survived for a long time in wet conditions could deteriorate rapidly after exposure. Removing it created obligations for treatment, storage and continued care. A museum display was not the automatic destination of every discovery. In some situations, recording and protecting material where it lay could be preferable. Decisions depended on vulnerability, research value, available expertise and the resources needed after excavation, not merely on whether an object would attract visitors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Community reports extended the team's reach. Walkers could notice new exposures between formal visits and submit photographs with the date and location. However, a photograph taken without a scale might not support a reliable measurement, and collecting an object could remove the context that made it informative. The project offered guidance on recording rather than encouraging a competition to retrieve finds. Reports were checked by specialists before being entered as confirmed observations in the public record.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Greyhaven's results were presented as a changing interpretation rather than a finished story of the inlet. New storms might reveal further evidence or destroy features already known. Repeated surveys made it possible to compare conditions over time, while a clear account of uncertainty allowed later researchers to revisit conclusions. The coastline's value as an archive lay not in preserving everything undisturbed, but in the possibility of carefully relating surviving traces to the processes that had altered them.

passages.title: When a number becomes a target

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Organisations need measurements. A hospital cannot plan its staffing without information about activity, and a delivery service needs to know whether parcels arrive. Yet a measurement used to describe a service can change its meaning when rewards depend on it. Staff may begin arranging work to improve the number, including in ways that do not improve the underlying service. This possibility does not make measurement pointless. It makes the connection between an indicator and its purpose a question to examine, rather than an assumption to forget.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In a fictional advice centre, managers initially counted completed appointments. The figure helped them estimate demand, but a new reward scheme paid teams for increasing it. Some appointments became shorter, and complex cases were divided into several visits. The total rose without a clear rise in the number of people whose problems were resolved. Nothing in the count showed whether this reflected deliberate gaming, legitimate changes in case complexity, or both. Further investigation was needed before judging the staff involved.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One proposed response was to replace appointment counts with satisfaction ratings. These added useful information, but they introduced other limitations. People who responded might differ from those who did not, and a pleasant encounter did not necessarily produce a lasting solution. Staff could also feel pressure to avoid giving unwelcome but accurate advice. The centre therefore treated satisfaction as one perspective on quality, not a direct substitute for every other measure. Replacing one imperfect indicator with another did not remove the need for judgment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The revised approach used a small group of indicators and reviewed difficult cases in detail. Managers examined access, waiting times, reported outcomes and staff accounts of obstacles. They avoided combining these immediately into a single score, because the trade-offs themselves were useful information. A shorter wait achieved by refusing complex cases would be visible as a change in access or outcomes. The system also allowed teams to explain unusual results instead of assuming that any deviation proved poor performance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Measurements had costs of their own. Recording more information took time away from direct work and created privacy risks if unnecessary personal details were retained. The centre removed fields that were rarely used and documented who needed access to the remaining records. Periodic reviews asked whether each indicator still supported a real decision. A dashboard could look comprehensive while containing information that nobody acted upon. Collecting it indefinitely was not evidence of a careful service.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The centre's experience suggests that the safest response to imperfect measures is neither blind faith nor complete rejection. Indicators can reveal problems and support learning when users know their limitations. They become less helpful when a target is treated as a definition of success and the behaviour it encourages is ignored. An effective measurement system should remain open to challenge, particularly when the numbers improve more quickly than the experience of the people it is meant to serve.

passages.title: The science of keeping a night sky dark

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Darkness is not simply the absence of useful lighting. For astronomers it makes faint objects visible; for some animals it provides a signal that helps organise activity. Outdoor light can serve essential purposes while also reaching places and times where it is not needed. The challenge is to distinguish illumination that supports a specific task from light that spills into a wider environment. A discussion framed only as a choice between safety and darkness misses many possible improvements in design and control.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In a fictional district called Bellmere, a lighting review began with a map of tasks. Staff identified crossings, entrances and working areas, then checked where existing lamps directed their light. Some illuminated empty upper walls more strongly than the paths below them. Shielding redirected output towards the intended surface. The review did not assume that every lamp needed replacing: changing its angle or adding a suitable shield could sometimes address the problem with fewer materials than installing a new fitting.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Brightness alone was an unreliable guide to visibility. Very bright sources could create glare, making nearby darker areas harder to see. Changes between bright and dark spaces also affected what pedestrians could notice. The team therefore assessed the pattern of lighting along a route instead of judging individual lamps in isolation. They invited residents to walk the routes and report difficult spots, while specialists checked the technical measurements. Personal experience and instrument readings answered related but different questions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Timing offered another opportunity. Some sites needed lighting throughout the night, whereas others were used only during a short period. Timers and carefully positioned sensors reduced unnecessary operation. However, a sensor that repeatedly switched a path into darkness could make the route uncomfortable or inaccessible. The review required a minimum level of appropriate lighting where continuous access was needed. Saving energy was one objective, but it could not be pursued by making legitimate users disappear from the plan.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The colour characteristics of light mattered too. Different sources emitted different mixtures of wavelengths, and their effects depended on the species, exposure and context being studied. The team avoided describing one colour label as harmless in every situation. It also distinguished electrical efficiency from environmental suitability: a source could use little electricity while still being badly positioned or used for too long. Efficient equipment made excessive lighting cheaper, which could even encourage additional installation unless total use was considered.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Bellmere monitored both energy consumption and reports about access after making changes. It recorded where darker conditions had been restored, rather than merely counting new lamps. The approach did not promise a completely unlit district. It aimed to provide the right light in the right place at the right time, with opportunities to correct mistakes. For the author, the central lesson is that reducing unwanted light can be a question of precision and restraint rather than a retreat from public safety.

passages.title: Who gets heard in a citizen survey?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A survey can contain many responses and still offer a distorted picture of a community. Its usefulness depends not only on the size of the dataset but also on who had an opportunity to respond and who chose to do so. Online questionnaires make participation convenient for some residents, while excluding others through language, access or confidence. Treating a large response total as proof of representativeness confuses the amount of information collected with the relationship between that information and the population of interest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the fictional town of Norfield, a consultation about a new park initially used a link on the council website. Responses strongly favoured sports facilities. The project team then compared the respondents with the area’s population and found that younger adults were overrepresented. This did not make their preferences invalid, but it weakened the claim that the result described everyone. The team needed to hear from groups who were missing before interpreting the balance of support across the town.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Researcher Lena Moss proposed recruiting through schools, older residents' groups and accessible community venues. These routes would not automatically create a perfect sample, but they could reach people absent from the original channel. She also suggested offering a short paper form and help in several languages. The aim was to widen the opportunity to participate without implying that everyone in a particular age or language group held the same opinion. Diversity within groups mattered as well as differences between them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Statistician Omar Ellis considered weighting: adjusting the contribution of responses to reflect known features of the population. This could reduce some imbalances, but it could not recover views that had never been captured. If residents with a particular barrier were absent entirely, giving more weight to the available respondents would not necessarily represent them. Ellis recommended publishing both the method and its limitations, rather than presenting a corrected number as though all uncertainty had been removed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Planner June Patel asked a different question: what should the survey decide? A popular preference might conflict with access requirements, budgets or ecological constraints. Residents should know which matters were open to choice and which were restricted by other responsibilities. Patel proposed combining preference questions with opportunities to explain practical needs. A small number of reports about an inaccessible entrance could be important even if most respondents did not mention it. The purpose was informed planning, not simply awarding the most votes a prize.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Norfield's final report presented the original responses, the additional recruitment and the remaining gaps separately. It did not merge them into an unexplained total. Readers could see how the evidence had developed and which conclusions were still tentative. The author argues that a consultation earns credibility by making its reach and limits visible. Listening well requires more than collecting enthusiastic answers; it requires checking whose silence has been mistaken for agreement.

passages.title: Learning from a forest without a control button

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A forest experiment differs from a laboratory experiment in a crucial way: researchers cannot reset the entire system between observations. Trees grow, organisms move, weather varies and past interventions leave traces. Scientists can still test hypotheses, but they need to consider what changes at the same time as the factor they hope to study. A result from one plot may be informative without being a reliable prediction for every forest. The challenge is to learn from local detail without disguising it as universal certainty.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At the fictional Rowan field station, a team investigated whether removing some undergrowth affected the survival of young trees. They selected several pairs of plots with broadly similar conditions. Within each pair, the treatment plot was chosen randomly and the other was left unchanged. The team measured survival before and after the intervention, rather than comparing only the final totals. This allowed them to account for some initial differences, although it could not guarantee that every relevant factor had been matched.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Scale complicated interpretation. A treatment that improved survival over one summer might have different effects after several dry years. Likewise, a small cleared area surrounded by dense vegetation might not behave like a large clearing. Seeds, shade and animal movement could cross the plot boundary. The researchers recorded neighbouring conditions and resisted describing a plot as a completely isolated unit. An experimental boundary helped organise the work; it did not stop ecological processes at its edge.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Technician Rosa Lin emphasised measurement consistency. If one observer counted a damaged seedling as alive while another counted it as dead, an apparent treatment effect might partly reflect a recording difference. The team agreed definitions, trained observers with shared examples and checked a sample of records independently. These checks did not make judgment unnecessary. They made disagreements visible so that the method could be improved before a large amount of incompatible data had accumulated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ecologist Ben Duarte argued for recording unexpected outcomes as well as the original survival measure. Removing vegetation might affect soil moisture, insect activity or browsing by animals. Such observations could suggest mechanisms or future questions. However, the team distinguished exploratory patterns from tests specified before seeing the data. A striking association discovered later could be worth following up without being presented as confirmation of a prediction nobody had actually made.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The Rowan report described the treatment, the site, the observation period and the uncertainty around the findings. It offered possible explanations but separated them from what had been directly measured. The author regards this restraint as a strength, not an admission that field research cannot produce knowledge. Useful findings become more transferable when readers understand the conditions under which they arose. A careful local experiment can contribute to a broader picture precisely because it does not claim to be the whole picture.

passages.title: Part 1 · A field course booking

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original teaching exercise, part one. A student books a weekend field course.
Coordinator: Hello, Northbank field centre. How may I help?
Student: I would like to join the weekend course. I first looked at birdwatching, but I have decided on coastal geology. The dates fit my schedule better.
Coordinator: Fine. May I have your surname?
Student: Mercer. M, E, R, C, E, R.
Coordinator: Thank you. The course begins on the eighteenth of September. The website previously showed the eleventh, but we changed it when the tutor became unavailable.
Student: Where should we meet? At the centre?
Coordinator: Not this time. Meet at the station entrance. Our minibus will collect the group there at eight forty-five. The course itself starts at nine thirty, so please use the collection time when planning your journey.
Student: Is accommodation included?
Coordinator: The basic fee includes transport during the course and the teaching materials, but not accommodation. We can give you a list of local places to stay. The field centre has no spare rooms that weekend.
Student: What should I bring?
Coordinator: A notebook is essential. We lend the measuring equipment, so there is no need to buy anything specialised. Bring waterproof clothing too. The route is mostly level, but the ground can be wet.
Student: How much is the deposit?
Coordinator: Twenty pounds. The balance is due a week before the course. If we cancel because of unsafe conditions, we refund the full payment. If you cancel, the conditions depend on how much notice you give; I will include those in the confirmation.
Student: I have a student card. Is there a reduced rate?
Coordinator: Yes, but we need a copy before issuing the final invoice. Please send it by email. Do not send your original card through the post.
Student: Will lunch be provided?
Coordinator: No, bring a packed lunch. There may be no shop near the field site. Drinking water is available at the centre before departure.
Student: That is clear. Please reserve a place.
Coordinator: I will send confirmation this afternoon.
This is the end of part one.

passages.title: Part 2 · The learning garden

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original teaching exercise, part two. A guide describes a learning garden. Use the labelled grid displayed with the questions. North is at the top. Rows run from west to east.
Welcome to the learning garden. You enter through the central gate at the south edge of the site. Before we explore, look at the simple plan. The squares are labelled A to I. A, B and C form the north row. D, E and F form the middle row, and G, H and I form the south row. The gate is at H.
The greenhouse is at B, in the centre of the north row. Some older leaflets put it in the northeast corner, but that space, C, now contains the pond. Please use the current plan rather than those leaflets.
Our tool store is at G, immediately west of the entrance gate. The compost area is at D, directly north of the tool store. The outdoor classroom occupies F, east of the central beds. These five places are the locations you need to mark.
Now for the activities. The first demonstration begins at ten fifteen. We used to begin at ten, but the earlier bus no longer runs, so we moved the start time. You can walk around beforehand, provided you remain on the paths.
The workshop today is free, although places must be reserved because space is limited. Donations are welcome, but they are not a condition of taking part. At the end, visitors can take home a packet of seeds. Please choose one packet per household so that there is enough for everyone.
If you bring children, remember that an adult must stay with them. Our staff lead activities, but the garden is not a drop-off childcare service. Near the pond, please keep younger children within reach.
We also ask everyone to stay on the marked paths. This protects the planting beds and helps us keep clear routes for other visitors. The paths may be wet, so shoes with a good grip are useful. If weather makes the outdoor classroom unsuitable, we will move the activity into the greenhouse and announce the change at the gate.
This is the end of part two.

passages.title: Part 3 · Choosing a research method

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original teaching exercise, part three. Two students discuss a small investigation with a supervisor.
Supervisor: You wanted to study how people use the library. What have you narrowed the question to?
Iris: We first thought about book borrowing, but the transaction data would be difficult to access. We now want to study how people choose study spaces.
Noah: We can observe which spaces are occupied at different times and then ask a few short questions about why people chose them.
Supervisor: Consider what each method can tell you. Observation can show where people sit, but not necessarily their reasons. Interviews can reveal reasons, but people may offer explanations that sound better than their actual decision process.
Iris: So we should compare the two rather than assume they will agree.
Supervisor: Yes. What is your sampling plan?
Noah: We will observe in the morning and the evening. We cannot cover the full day, so we will explain that limitation in the report. Initially we planned to study only during exam week, but that would be an unusual period. We will collect the main data during an ordinary teaching week instead.
Iris: Our pilot showed another problem. We both counted an occupied desk differently. I counted a bag as evidence that someone was using the space, but Noah counted only people who were physically present.
Supervisor: You need a shared definition. Record desks with unattended belongings separately from desks with a person present. Do not silently mix those categories.
Noah: We will revise the observation sheet before collecting more data.
Supervisor: Good. And how will you handle interviews?
Iris: Participation will be voluntary. We will not record names or student numbers. We will ask permission to quote an anonymous response in the report.
Supervisor: Keep the questions neutral. Instead of asking why the quiet room is obviously better, ask which features mattered in the choice. Also make clear that you are students doing an assignment, not library staff checking whether people belong there.
Noah: We will do that. Our deadline is Friday, but we can send the revised questions by Tuesday.
Supervisor: Please send them on Tuesday. That gives us time to review them before recruitment.
This is the end of part three.

passages.title: Part 4 · The work of an urban archive

paragraphs.label: Transcript
paragraphs.text:
This is an original teaching exercise, part four. A lecturer discusses the organisation of a fictional city archive.
An archive is not simply a room full of old objects. It is a collection whose value depends heavily on context. A photograph without a date or location may still be interesting, but it can be harder to use as evidence. Archivists therefore preserve information about an item as well as the item itself.
One important concept is provenance: the record of where material came from and how it entered the collection. This helps later users evaluate what the material can support. It should not be confused with proof that every statement in the material is true. A well-documented personal diary can contain mistakes, memories or opinions.
Cataloguing makes material discoverable. A useful catalogue may include subject terms and an explanation of the original arrangement. However, modern labels can introduce assumptions that were absent from the original records. Staff should distinguish their description from language found in the source, especially where historical terms require explanation.
Digitisation can widen access, but it does not remove the need for conservation. The original may still contain physical evidence that an image fails to capture. Digital files also need maintenance: storage systems change, files can become damaged and formats may become difficult to open. Backup copies should be checked, not merely created and forgotten.
In our fictional example, volunteers helped transcribe handwritten letters. The project used shared examples to explain how to handle uncertain words. Volunteers marked uncertainty rather than silently guessing. A second reader checked the work before a transcription was released as verified. This method did not eliminate every error, but it made checking part of the process.
Access also involved ethical choices. Some collections contained personal information about people who might still be affected by publication. The archive reviewed restrictions and explained why certain items were not available online. Making everything searchable immediately would not automatically have been responsible access.
Finally, the archive kept a revision history for catalogue entries. When new evidence changed an interpretation, readers could see what had changed and why. The collection was not less valuable because its descriptions developed. Its credibility depended partly on preserving a clear route from the surviving material to the claims made about it.
This is the end of part four.

writing.title: 通勤方式的变化
writing.prompt: The chart shows the percentage of commuters using three modes of transport in the fictional city of Arden between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.analysis: 动态图：先比较方向，再看排序变化；时间过去，用过去时。
ideas: 汽车下降，铁路和自行车上升。
汽车始终最多，但与铁路差距缩小。
2000→2020 汽车减少 20 个百分点，不是减少 20%。
outline: 引言改写城市、比例与时间。
Overview：变化方向与持续领先者。
主体一：汽车与铁路起终点及差距。
主体二：自行车的增长，作适量比较。
writing.sample:
The line chart compares the proportions of commuters travelling by car, rail and bicycle in the fictional city of Arden from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, car use declined, whereas both rail travel and cycling became more common. Cars nevertheless remained the most widely used of the three modes throughout the period, although their lead over rail narrowed considerably.

In 2000, 65% of commuters used cars, compared with 20% who travelled by rail. The figure for cars fell at every subsequent observation, reaching 56% in 2010 and 45% in 2020. Rail followed the opposite pattern, rising to 27% halfway through the period and ending at 35%. Consequently, the gap between these two modes decreased from 45 to 10 percentage points.

Cycling accounted for a much smaller proportion of journeys, but its share also increased steadily. Starting at 5%, it reached 10% in 2010 and finished at 15%, three times its initial level. Despite this growth, cycling remained less common than either of the other modes in the final year.
errors: Overview 提炼主要趋势，不把所有数字重述一遍。
区分百分比变化与百分点差异；不补充图中没有的原因。
writing.source: 本站原创题目与虚构数据；图表为教学设计。
writing.review: 教学示例，非考官认证范文；不标注分数。

writing.sample:
The diagram illustrates a simplified sequence in which used paper is converted into recycled paper.

Overall, the process consists of six main stages, beginning with the collection of discarded paper and ending with the production of dry paper. Between these points, the material is sorted, mixed with water and cleaned before it is pressed and dried.

At the first stage, used paper is collected so that it can enter the recycling process. The collected material is then sorted. After this preparation, water is added to the paper to form pulp. These initial steps change the material from separate pieces of discarded paper into a mixture that can be processed further.

Next, the pulp passes through a cleaning stage. The cleaned material is subsequently pressed, after which it moves to the final drying stage. Once drying is complete, recycled paper is produced. The diagram presents these operations as a single sequence and does not show a return to any earlier stage or provide information about the time required for individual steps.

writing.prompt: Some people believe that public transport should be free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

writing.sample:
Making public transport free is an appealing way to reduce travel costs. Although I support substantial help for people who struggle to afford essential journeys, I do not think removing fares for every passenger should be the main priority in all cities.

There is a strong case for reducing the cost of transport for those who depend on it. A person looking for work, for example, may need to travel to several interviews before receiving any income. Even modest fares can restrict the opportunities available to that person. Discounted passes or free travel for low-income residents could address this barrier directly. Similar support may help students and people attending regular medical appointments. These benefits justify public funding, particularly when the assistance reaches people whose choices are otherwise limited.

However, fares are only one reason people avoid buses or trains. A free service that runs infrequently or fails to arrive on time may still be unsuitable for someone who must reach work at a fixed hour. If abolishing fares reduces the money available for maintenance and additional services, passengers could gain financially while losing a useful transport option. In a city with limited resources, improving reliability and providing accessible stops may therefore bring greater practical benefits than subsidising passengers who can already afford to pay.

The appropriate policy should also reflect local conditions. A small network with spare capacity faces different pressures from an overcrowded system that needs major investment. Governments should compare these needs rather than assume that one fare policy suits every place.

In conclusion, affordable travel is an important public goal, but universal free transport is not always the best route to it. I would prioritise targeted support alongside dependable, well-funded services, so that lower costs translate into journeys people can actually make.

writing.title: 远程办公
writing.prompt: More employees now work from home rather than travelling to an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
writing.analysis: 必须称量而非只列利弊；可限定适合岗位。

例子用于解释机制，不编造机构、调查或精确统计。

writing.sample:
The growth of home working has changed how many employees organise their day. In my view, its advantages generally outweigh its disadvantages for jobs that can be performed remotely, provided that employers make deliberate arrangements for collaboration and support.

The clearest benefit is the removal of the daily commute. An employee who previously spent a long time travelling can use some of that time for rest, family responsibilities or focused work. Remote arrangements may also widen access to employment. Someone who cannot move to an expensive city, for instance, may still be able to contribute to an organisation based there. These gains concern both personal well-being and the range of people an employer can recruit. They are especially valuable when performance can be judged by completed work rather than physical presence.

The main disadvantages involve communication and learning. A new colleague may find it harder to ask small questions when every conversation requires a scheduled call. Informal exchanges can also help teams notice problems before they become serious. Furthermore, working in the same place as one lives can make it difficult to stop at the end of the day. These are substantial concerns, and simply supplying a laptop does little to solve them.

Nevertheless, the problems are not equally severe in every remote arrangement. Regular mentoring, agreed hours of availability and occasional meetings with a clear purpose can preserve support while retaining much of the flexibility. Such measures cannot turn every occupation into a remote job, but they can improve the experience of employees whose duties allow it.

Overall, I consider the savings in travel time and the broader access to suitable jobs more important than the disadvantages in this context. The benefits are strongest when remote work is treated as a considered organisational choice, with attention to how people learn and cooperate.
